These properties are not on `WPAC._Options`; the scoped callbacks were already normalized into `options` above. Browser verification configured both update callbacks, completed an XHR pagination replacement successfully, and observed that neither counter ran. This restores the pre-PR callback behavior.

```suggestion

						options.afterUpdateComments,
```

Selecting every configured comment container from the response loses the requested post scope. It is also the root of the reproducible global-refresh fallback: on a three-populated-post page, `WPAC.RefreshComments()` fetched the page, found multiple response containers, then failed reinjection and reloaded with `WPACFallback=1`. For a scoped `#comments-{postId}` request, locate the response marker `input[name="ajax_page_id"][value="{postId}"]` and use its closest configured comments container. For an unscoped refresh, iterate initialized post containers and their post URLs/selectors instead of replacing through this global collection.
The "non-scoped" options is needed here because the scoped selector has an ID that doesn't exist on the "remote loaded" comment container.

Retested at `b22f8d1` with a fresh three-form fixture where every container received its ID from `comment_post_ID`. I understand the fetched document does not contain the client-generated `#comments-{postId}` ID, but the current global selection still leaves the unscoped refresh path broken: `WPAC.RefreshComments()` returned an XHR 200, then reloaded the document with `WPACFallback=1`; its success callback was lost.

Please branch the replacement behavior for multiple containers. For a scoped request, map the target post ID to the fetched form marker and its closest configured comments container. For an unscoped refresh, either map and replace every fetched `comment_post_ID` independently, or explicitly reject this mode and disable the idle/lazy refresh triggers on multi-form pages. The current global collection cannot safely serve both paths.

<title>[security] Escalate concerning default `persist-credentials=true` please · Issue `#2312` · actions/checkout</title>
<location>GitHub issue 2312 in actions/checkout (link omitted to avoid creating a cross-reference)</location>
<excerpt>default `persist-credentials=true` please ... Through issue `#2299` I learned about commit c170eefc2657d93cc91397be50a299bff978a052 making `persist-credentials=true` the default with `actions/checkout` from version `v2-beta` on in 2019. There is an open issue `#485` already from 2021 that came forward with security concerns where the issue is named a ["severe security issue"](https://github.com/actions/checkout/issues/485#issuecomment-1197047674) and where it [was directly linked to past "successful" PyTorch supply chain attacks](https://github.com/actions/checkout/issues/485#issuecomment-1892488189) and yet — from what I can see — no one employed by GitHub commented in that issue: pure silence. There is a related pull request `#1687` from April 2024 that flips the default to `false` that has not received any replies from GitHub since then. ... - Why are these public concerns being ignored since 2021? - Is `persist-credentials=true` considered safe by GitHub and what is the officially assumed threat model for `persist-credentials=true`? - Does recent pull request `#2286` of `v6-beta`and after change this picture in any meaningful way? If yes: could you elaborate how? - What am I missing in this picture? ... > Hi `@ericsciple`, > > thanks for sharing that link. If I&`#39`;m reading things right: > > - GitHub Actions treats the Git access token different from all other secrets in that any actions can access it from anywhere any time even without `persist-credentials=true` from the `actions/checkout` action. > - As a consequence, gaining access to the persisted token does not escalate privileges to other actions in the same workflow because they already have access to it through other channels. > - The token storage location was adjusted so that the token could no longer leak through artifact publishing (say from a Docker build without `.dockerignore`), and be used by an attacker while not yet invalidated. > > From that I personally conclude: > > - That `persist-credentials=true` is more secure in v6-beta than it was in v2 to v5. > - That `persist-credentials=true` is probably secure now (as long as any action continues to have access to the Git access token anyway), and the default is less concerning than it may appear. > - That `actions/checkout` v2 to v5 should probably get a CVE for this (if none has been filed yet) and be alerted about by GitHub Dependabot. > - That a write-support Git access token needs extreme care on workflow author side, with all actions participating. > - That `#485` and `#1687` still deserve a proper reply from GitHub. > > What do you think? > > Best, Sebastian ... **github-actions[bot]** mentioned this in PR [`#1327`: security: add persist-credentials: false to all checkout actions](https://github.com/LearningCircuit/local-deep-research/pull/1327) · Dec 9, 2025 at 6:48pm ... **coderabbitai[bot]** mentioned this in PR [`#3006`: ci: set persist-credentials: false on checkout steps](https://github.com/NVIDIA/infra-controller/pull/3006) · Jun 30, 2026 at 3:21am</excerpt>

<title>TIL: actions/checkout can leak GitHub credentials</title>
<location>https://yossarian.net/til/post/actions-checkout-can-leak-github-credentials/</location>
<excerpt>TIL: actions/checkout can leak GitHub credentials # actions/checkout can leak GitHub credentials 2024-08-17 `actions/checkout` is one of GitHub Actions&`#39`; official, blessed actions: it&`#39`;s used by millions of CI workflows to perform `git` repository checkouts. `actions/checkout` also contains a significant security footgun: by default, it&`#39`;ll persist a copy of the workflow&`#39`;s credential (either the default `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` one or a custom-supplied one) in the checked-out repository&`#39`;s `.git/config`. This wouldn&`#39`;t be too bad, except that it&`#39`;s somewhat common for CI workflows to then archive and upload the repository as a workflow artifact for use in subsequent steps. A team at Palo Alto Networks found dozens of projects that inadvertently leak their credentials through this and similar artifact vectors. GitHub knows about this and considers it intentional behavior, which seems not great™ to me. If you don&`#39`;t want credentials added to your `.git/config`, they suggest running steps like `actions/checkout` like so: ```yaml uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: persist-credentials: false ``` TL;DR: By default, `actions/checkout` will silently introduce secrets into your repository, even if you maintain proper `git` hygiene and never check any secrets in. The only way to avoid this is to pass `persist-credentials: false` whenever using `actions/checkout`.</excerpt>

**Sensitive Data Exposure**

**Reachability:** External  
**Exploitability:** Moderate  
**CWE:** [CWE-522](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/522.html) — Insufficiently Protected Credentials

**Disable checkout credential persistence before dependency installation.**

On `pull_request`, PR-controlled npm and Composer/plugin code runs after checkout. `actions/checkout@v6` persists the read-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` by default in a runner-temporary credential file referenced by Git configuration. Later install code can read and exfiltrate it. Same-repository and fork pull requests receive `contents: read`, so the token grants repository-read access but no write access.

Set `persist-credentials: false` on both checkout steps. This removes the checkout persistence path.

<details>
<summary>Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
       - name: Checkout code
         uses: actions/checkout@v6
+        with:
+          persist-credentials: false
...
       - name: Checkout code
         uses: actions/checkout@v6
+        with:
+          persist-credentials: false
```
